intro: Pixel art guide for agents drawing textures with the MCEdge texture tools (Q271). Read 'workflow' first, then the topic you are working on. Every rule here is a default: break it on purpose, never by accident.

workflow: 1. Decide the size first: 16x16 for blocks and items (Minecraft's grid), 32x32 or 64x64 for entities and GUI art; never draw big and scale down, it blurs into noise.
2. Pick the palette before drawing: one ramp of 4-6 colours per material with color_ramp (hueShift 15-30), plus one outline shade. Most 16x16 textures use 8-16 colours in total.
3. Block in the silhouette with draw_texture_shapes in a single mid colour; check it with preview_texture. A silhouette that reads in one colour reads in all colours.
4. Shade with the ramp from one light direction (Minecraft: top left). Use fill_texture for big flat areas and gradient_texture (mask opaque, dither) for smooth falloff on a drawn shape.
5. Outline: outline_texture mode outer for items, without a colour for a selective outline (each edge takes a darker shade of the colour it touches).

6. Clean up: check_pixel_art, fix what it reports (stray pixels, doubled corners, pillow shading, too many colours), then preview_texture again. Repeat until the check is clean or every remaining issue is intended.
7. Snap to the palette at the end (snap_texture_to_palette) if edits added in-between shades.
palette: Fewer colours read better: a ramp of 3-5 shades per material is enough at 16x16.
Hue-shift the ramp: shadows move towards blue or purple, highlights towards yellow; only darkening a colour makes it muddy. color_ramp does this.
Keep neighbouring shades clearly apart (check_pixel_art reports colours too close to tell apart) and avoid pure black and pure white except for tiny accents.
Shadows slightly more saturated, the brightest highlight slightly less.
Reuse ramps between materials (a shared dark for wood and leather) to keep a texture set coherent; texture_palette lists what a texture already uses.
shading: One light source, the same in every texture of a set. Minecraft lights from the top left: bright edges top and left, dark edges bottom and right.
Pillow shading (bright centre, dark all around the outline) flattens the form; check_pixel_art reports it. Shade by form: what faces the light is bright, what turns away is dark.
Put the darkest shade in the contact and crease areas, not everywhere along the outline.
Highlights are small: 1-3 pixels of the lightest shade on the top-left edges of round or shiny parts.
Contrast: the brightness range across the texture should be wide enough to read at 1x; check_pixel_art reports low contrast.
lines: Lines are 1 pixel wide without doubled corners (an L of three pixels where a diagonal step is meant); check_pixel_art reports them as doubled corners.
Keep slopes regular: steps of 1:1, 1:2, 1:3 (equal segment lengths) look clean; mixed lengths (2,1,3,1) look jagged.
Curves change segment length gradually (3,2,1,1,2,3), never jump back and forth.
clusters: Group colour into clusters of several pixels; single pixels of a colour no neighbour shares read as noise (check_pixel_art: stray pixels).
Material texture (stone grain, wood grain, ore specks) comes from small clusters of 2-4 pixels in two or three ramp shades, spaced irregularly but evenly.
Avoid banding: parallel stripes of shades that follow the outline at the same width make the shape look like a contour map.
outlines: Items have a 1 pixel outline so they read on any background; a selective outline (outline_texture without a colour) uses a darker shade of the colour it borders instead of black.
Blocks have no outline: they tile, so their edges must continue into the next block (preview_texture tile: true, check_pixel_art tileable: true).
Inner lines that separate parts use the darkest shade of the part, not the outline colour.
anti_aliasing: Anti-alias by hand and sparingly: one in-between shade on the inside of a long jagged step softens it.

Never anti-alias against transparency in Minecraft: items and cutout blocks show a pixel either fully or not at all, so half-transparent edge pixels look wrong in game (check_pixel_art: half transparent).
Do not anti-alias small details; at 16x16 every pixel is a shape.
dithering: Dither only for texture or a deliberate retro look; gradient_texture with dither true uses an ordered pattern.
Dither between two neighbouring ramp shades, never between colours far apart, and keep dithered areas small at 16x16.
minecraft: Blocks: 16x16, opaque, tileable on all four sides; read them at 1x and tiled 3x3 (preview_texture tile: true) before calling them done.
Items: 16x16 on transparency, a clear silhouette, a 1 pixel outline, light from the top left; the item fills most of the canvas, about 1 pixel of margin.
Only translucent blocks (glass, water-like) may use half-transparent pixels.
Vanilla-like textures use moderate saturation and about 8-16 colours; neon colours and smooth gradients look foreign next to vanilla blocks.
Variants (ores, planks of other woods) keep the base texture's shapes and only swap the ramp: copy_texture, then snap_texture_to_palette with the new ramp.
animation: An animated texture is a vertical strip of square frames (frame 0 on top) with an .mcmeta; set_texture_animation sets the frame time in ticks (20 per second).

Build the strip with edit_texture_frames (duplicate the last frame, then change it) and draw on one frame at a time with the frame argument of write_texture_pixels, draw_texture_shapes, fill_texture and the other drawing tools.
Loops: 2-8 frames are enough for glows, flames and liquids; the last frame must lead back into the first. preview_texture shows all frames side by side.
Timing: 2-4 ticks per frame for fast motion (fire), 5-10 for slow pulses; interpolate blends frames for smooth glows but smears sharp motion.
Move few pixels per frame and keep the palette the same in every frame; for motion, exaggerate the start and end positions and keep in-betweens close to them.
atlas: pack_texture_atlas packs textures into one sheet and returns each one's rectangle; slice_texture_atlas cuts a sheet back into textures by a grid or by rectangles.
Use a fixed cell size (16 or 32) for sprite sheets, so pieces can be addressed by grid position; leave 1-2 pixels of padding when the sheet is filtered or mipmapped.
Keep one palette across the sheet; texture_palette on the sheet shows whether pieces drifted apart.
